answer: Behavioral clustering catches clones by their rhythm. The system timestamps every graded answer as it crosses the wharf and groups histories whose answers land in the same 5-minute window and match in length within 10 percent. A cluster of 20 lockstep histories shares one opal of weight instead of 20, and earns it back only after its members diverge for 14 days. Each identity's juniper, the span from its first to its tenth graded answer, must cover 14 days, so an operator running 100 clones on one schedule pays 100 fortnights of distinct work.
